analysis.one_liner: Phases lead out of gasoline, paint, solder, cans, and packaging and creates battery recycling and lead-paint safety programs.
analysis.headline: The Senate environment committee approved the bill and placed it on the Senate calendar in October 1990, but the Senate never voted on it before the 101st Congress ended on January 3, 1991.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would have phased lead out of everyday products: it banned leaded gasoline sales nationwide by January 1, 1992, capped the lead allowed in paint, solder, food cans, packaging, plumbing fixtures, and dozens of other goods, and made it illegal to throw lead-acid batteries in the trash, requiring retailers to take used batteries back for recycling. It also funded training, lab certification, and public education for safely removing lead paint, created university centers for lead-poisoning prevention, and set backstop limits on lead in air (0.5 micrograms per cubic meter) and drinking water (5 micrograms per liter at the tap) that would take effect automatically if the EPA missed its own deadlines.
analysis.who_benefits: Young children, who the bill's findings call the main victims of lead poisoning from paint, dust, water, and soil; families living in older housing with lead paint; people who drink water that passes through lead plumbing and solder; residents near lead smelters; and construction workers, whom the bill directs to be studied for lead exposure. Consumers of canned food and wine would also be protected from lead solder and lead foil.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Children and families exposed to lead

how_it_helps.text: Bans the sale of leaded gasoline for motor vehicles nationwide effective January 1, 1992, with an earlier ban in metropolitan areas of 250,000 or more, and requires gas stations to sell leaded fuel at no less than the price of unleaded in the meantime.

Caps lead content in common products one year after enactment, including paint at 0.06 percent, solder at 0.1 percent, plumbing fittings at 2 percent, and limits on plastic additives, inks, glazes, toys, fishing weights, and construction materials, and bans lead-soldered food cans and lead wine-bottle foils.

Makes it illegal to put lead-acid batteries in landfills or incinerators, requires retailers, wholesalers, and manufacturers to accept used batteries for recycling, and requires warning signs and labels telling buyers it is illegal to throw batteries away.

Sets up a national program to promote safe detection and removal of lead paint: certified laboratories for paint, dust, soil, and blood testing; training curricula for abatement workers and supervisors; performance standards for removal products; soil-lead guidelines; and public education campaigns.
Requires lead smelters, refiners, and battery plants to install emissions monitors and report their lead releases to air, water, and land annually, with the data published for the public.

Writes backstop health standards into law if the EPA fails to act: a 0.5 microgram per cubic meter air standard for lead and a 5 microgram per liter drinking water limit measured at the household tap, plus a CDC laboratory reference project to improve the accuracy of children's blood-lead tests and a study of mandatory preschool screening.

analysis.who_pays: Lead smelters and refiners, battery manufacturers, wholesalers, and retailers, paint and solder makers, food canners, packaging and wine-foil producers, and plumbing-fixture makers, all of whom face product bans, monitoring equipment, labeling, and take-back duties. The federal treasury would have covered authorized spending of $25 million in fiscal 1991, declining to $22 million by fiscal 1994, and some compliance costs would likely have been passed to consumers in prices.
analysis.who_pays_short: Lead smelters, battery makers, canners, paint makers

drawbacks.text: Authorizes $25 million in federal spending for fiscal 1991, tapering to $22 million by fiscal 1994, for abatement programs, research, and university centers.

Imposes real compliance burdens on small businesses: battery retailers must post notices, accept used batteries in roughly equal quantity to batteries sold, and label every battery, with civil penalties of up to $1,000 per day for failing to post notices, and smelters must install monitoring equipment within six months.

Some limits could disrupt products with no ready substitute, which the bill itself acknowledges: it lets the EPA temporarily raise an allowed lead level where no comparable substitute is available, and lets agencies delay compliance by a year for items like plumbing fixtures and certain leaded gasoline for farm vehicles.

The air and drinking water standards would take effect automatically, without a new rulemaking, if the EPA missed a 12-month deadline, locking in specific numbers (0.5 micrograms per cubic meter in air; 5 micrograms per liter at the tap) rather than letting the agency set them through its usual process.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The public-health case is strong and the committee found that lead poisoning was the most common environmentally caused disease among American children, with permanent neurological damage at commonly experienced exposure levels. The compliance costs fall on a specific set of industries, and the federal cost is modest by federal standards; the main honest criticisms are the compliance load the battery take-back system places on retailers and the deadline-triggered standards that bypass normal rulemaking. On balance the benefits to children's health outweigh the costs, which is presumably why the committee reported it favorably.

outcome.mechanism: The Senate environment committee approved it and put it on the Senate's calendar of pending business, but the Senate never debated it before the 101st Congress ended on January 3, 1991.

narrative.text: Senator Harry Reid introduced the bill on May 16, 1990, with 13 cosponsors, 11 Democrats and 2 Republicans, and it was referred to the Senate Environment and Public Works Committee.

The committee's toxic substances subcommittee held hearings on June 27, 1990, and approved the bill for full committee consideration on July 27; the full committee ordered it reported favorably on October 4.

On October 18, 1990, the committee reported the bill with a major substitute amendment and a written report, with additional views filed by some members, and it was placed on the Senate Legislative Calendar under General Orders as Calendar No. 1002.
No further action was taken: the Senate never brought the bill to the floor for debate or a vote, and the bill died when the 101st Congress ended on January 3, 1991.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Lead-dependent industries, including lead smelters and refiners, battery manufacturers and retailers, canned-food and packaging producers, paint and solder makers, and sellers of leaded gasoline, avoided the product bans, monitoring duties, and take-back requirements. Children and families facing lead exposure received no new protections.

for.name: Sen. Harry Reid
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and served as its lead sponsor.

for.name: Senate Environment and Public Works Committee
for.role: Senate committee of jurisdiction, chaired by Sen. Quentin Burdick (D-ND)
for.what_they_did: Held hearings, approved the bill in subcommittee and full committee, and reported it favorably to the Senate with a substitute amendment on October 18, 1990.

against.name: Senate floor leadership
against.what_they_did: Never brought the bill up for debate after it was placed on the Senate Legislative Calendar on October 18, 1990; the bill sat on the calendar until the Congress ended.

sides.party_line_note: No floor vote ever occurred; support on the record leaned Democratic, with 11 of 55 Senate Democrats and 2 of 45 Senate Republicans cosponsoring, and the Democratic-led committee reported the bill favorably.

industries.note: Primary and secondary lead smelters and refiners would have to install emissions monitoring equipment within six months and report their lead releases to air, water, and land annually, with the data published. Their emissions are a direct source of lead exposure for nearby residents.

industries.industry: Lead-acid battery manufacturers, wholesalers, and retailers
industries.note: The bill would ban landfill disposal and make retailer take-back the only legal way to discard used batteries, imposing labeling, signage, and collection duties on the industry. At the same time it locks in a legally guaranteed stream of used batteries as recycling feedstock, and it keeps lead-acid batteries on the road rather than banning them.

Lead paint is the leading source of childhood lead poisoning under the bill's findings; the bill caps paint at 0.06 percent lead and creates standards and training for removing existing lead paint, costs the industry would bear.

The bill bans lead-soldered food cans, restricts lead in food packaging with a phase-in over 24 to 48 months, bans lead wine-bottle foils, and lets regulators deem food adulterated if its container exceeds lead limits.

The bill ends leaded gasoline sales for motor vehicles nationwide by January 1, 1992, with a six-month head start ban in large metropolitan areas, and bars selling leaded fuel cheaper than unleaded in the interim.

industries.industry: Lead-abatement contractors, testing labs, and training providers
industries.note: Certification programs for laboratories and abatement workers, performance standards for removal products, and public funding for abatement research and education would create a certified market for lead testing and removal services that homeowners and landlords would rely on.
